'''''Stapelia gigantea''''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the genus ''[[Stapelia]]'' of the family [[Apocynaceae]].<ref name=WCSP_512006/> Common names include [[carrion plant]] and '''toad plant''' (although the nickname "carrion plant" can also refer to ''[[Stapelia grandiflora]]''). The plant is native to the desert regions of northeastern [[South Africa]] (KwaZulu-Natal and Northern Provinces) north to [[Malawi]] and [[Zambia]].<ref name="POWO">{{cite POWO |title=''Stapelia gigantea'' N.E.Br. |id=101594-1 |access-date=2025-07-04}}</ref>

==Description==
Growing up to {{cvt|25|cm|in|0}} tall, it is a clump-forming [[succulent plant]] with erect green four-angled stems {{cvt|3|cm}} thick. The flowers are large, up to {{cvt|40|cm|0}} wide, star-shaped, with five petals.<ref name="PlantZAfrica">{{cite web | title=Stapelia gigantea | website=PlantZAfrica | date=2021-03-21 | url=https://pza.sanbi.org/stapelia-gigantea | access-date=2025-07-04}}</ref> The flowers are red and yellow, wrinkled, with a silky texture and fringed with hairs, that can be as long as {{cvt|8|mm|in|1}}. They flower throughout the year, but most prolifically in late summer, between December and April in South Africa.<ref name="PlantZAfrica"/>

The flowers have the smell of rotting flesh,<ref name="RHSAZ">{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|pages=1136}}</ref> in order to attract the flies which [[pollen|pollinate]] them. Scent compounds of carrion flowers responsible for their odour include diamines ([[putrescine]] and [[cadaverine]]), sulfur compounds and various phenolic molecules.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Benbow |first1=M. Eric |last2=Tomberlin |first2=Jeffery K. |last3=Tarone |first3=Aaron M. |title=Carrion Ecology, Evolution, and Their Applications |date=August 2015 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=9780429102240 |page=373}}</ref> Because of the foul odour of its flower, ''S. gigantea'' can act as an appetite suppressant in humans.<ref>{{Citation|last1=Corley|first1=David Gregory|title=Plant derived or derivable material with appetite suppressing activity|date=Mar 7, 2006|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US7008648|last2=Miller|first2=James|access-date=2016-09-28}}</ref>

There have been several proposed reasons for the size of the flowers of ''S. gigantea''. First, it is possible that they are large to attract the flies that pollinate them.<ref name="Johnson">{{Cite journal|last=Johnson, and Jurgens|title=Convergent evolution of carrion and faecal scent mimicry in fly-pollinated angiosperm flowers and a stinkhorn fungus.|journal=South African Journal of Botany|date=2010 |volume=76 |issue=4 |page=796 |doi=10.1016/j.sajb.2010.07.012 |bibcode=2010SAJB...76..796J |doi-access=free }}</ref> The large size and colour of the flowers combined with the carrion smell may cause the flies to behave as if it is a dead carcass and be more likely to visit it.<ref name="Johnson" /><ref name=Endress>{{Cite journal|last=Davis Endress, and Baum.|title=The evolution of floral gigantism|journal=Current Opinion in Plant Biology | volume=11 | doi=10.1016/j.pbi.2007.11.003 | pmid=18207449 | year=2008|issue=1|pages=49–57 |bibcode=2008COPB...11...49D }}</ref>

==Ecology==
''Stapelia gigantea'' grows in arid areas, often on sandy soil or rocky outcrops, and often with little other vegetation, though also sometimes in or even under open shubs. In South Africa, it occurs at altitudes from 325–1,100 m.<ref name="PlantZAfrica"/>

''S. gigantea'' can become an invasive plant when introduced in arid and semi-arid environments, although it has been found to facilitate the recruitment of [[ecological facilitation|nurse-dependent]] native taxa, those that require a suitable microhabitat created by another plant for successful germination, growth, and/or survival from impacts such as [[herbivory]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Herrera|first1=Ileana|last2=Ferrer-Paris|first2=José R.|last3=Hernández-Rosas|first3=José I.|last4=Nassar|first4=Jafet M.|title=Impact of two invasive succulents on native-seedling recruitment in Neotropical arid environments|journal=Journal of Arid Environments|date=2016|volume=132|pages=15–25|doi=10.1016/j.jaridenv.2016.04.007|bibcode=2016JArEn.132...15H |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/301927334|accessdate=6 May 2016}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
Since it does not tolerate temperatures below {{convert|10|C|F|abbr=on}} for extended periods, this plant must be grown under glass in [[temperateness|temperate]] zones. It has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Stapelia gigantea''|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/17744/Stapelia-gigantea/Details | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 99 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 21 November 2018}}</ref> The [[cultivar]] 'Zulu Giant' is often grown.
